report:
**Conclusion:** No—dexamethasone and related systemic corticosteroids do not *ensure* survival, but strong randomized-trial evidence shows they **reduce the risk of death** in hospitalized patients with severe/critical COVID-19 who need oxygen or mechanical ventilation.

In the RECOVERY randomized trial, dexamethasone lowered 28-day mortality by about one-third in patients on invasive ventilation (rate ratio 0.64) and by about one-fifth in those receiving oxygen without invasive ventilation (0.82). It did **not** help—and might harm—patients who did not require respiratory support. [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2021436)

A prospective meta-analysis of seven randomized trials in critically ill patients likewise found lower 28-day all-cause mortality with systemic corticosteroids than with usual care/placebo. [https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2770279)

A Cochrane review concludes that systemic corticosteroids probably reduce mortality modestly overall in symptomatic hospitalized COVID-19, while uncertainty remains about the best specific drug, dose, and regimen. [https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD014963/abstract](https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD014963/abstract)

Thus, these drugs are an important, evidence-based treatment for oxygen-requiring or critically ill patients, but they are not a guarantee and should be prescribed and monitored by clinicians because they can cause adverse effects (for example, high blood glucose and secondary infections).
